Female Linguado (Paralichthys orbignyanus) attain a maximum documented total length of 83 centimeters [Li = 83 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the larger flatfishes inhabiting the subtropical coastal waters of the southwestern Atlantic. Growth trajectories derived from otolith-based age assignments indicate that individuals approach this asymptotic length only after several years of sustained feeding on a diet dominated by demersal fish and crustaceans. The length-weight relationship for this species, conventionally expressed as W = aL^b, yields an estimated ultimate wet weight of 6000 grams [Wwi = 6000 grams] for a female achieving the maximum length, reflecting the substantial somatic investment required to reach such dimensions. Field records also show that the onset of sexual maturity, as determined by histological examination of gonadal tissue, occurs at a total length of 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters]. At this length, females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to initiate vitellogenesis, and the corresponding body mass at this developmental milestone is approximately 578.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 578.4 grams], a value derived from the same length-weight power function that describes the species' allometry.

The reproductive strategy of Linguado involves a pronounced seasonal spawning period that coincides with elevated autumn water temperatures in the Patos Lagoon estuary, a primary nursery ground for this species. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable thermal regime of 16.1 °C [T = 16.1 °C], females exhibit a maximum reproductive output with approximately 110 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 110 eggs per spawning event] and multiple spawnings per season [F_R_i = multiple spawnings per season], reflecting the combined influence of batch fecundity and spawning interval. This daily production is partitioned across multiple spawning events within a single reproductive season, with each gravid female releasing successive batches of pelagic eggs. The temperature of 16.1 °C appears to represent an optimal thermal window for gametogenesis and oocyte maturation, as rates of egg production decline markedly when individuals are held at temperatures exceeding 20 °C. This thermal sensitivity underscores the potential vulnerability of this species to warming coastal waters linked to climate change.

At the earliest stage of life, recently fertilized eggs, based on a congeneric species, measure between 0.7 and 0.8 millimeters in diameter, and from this egg size the wet weight at birth for Linguado is estimated 0.00022 grams [Wwb = estimated 0.00022 grams]. This minuscule initial mass is characteristic of pelagic-spawning flatfishes, which produce large numbers of small, yolk-dependent eggs that undergo rapid embryonic development. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins, at which point the larva must successfully capture its first prey to avoid starvation. The duration of this lecithotrophic phase is strongly temperature-dependent, with warmer conditions accelerating yolk absorption but also increasing the risk of reaching the point of no reserve before suitable zooplankton prey are encountered. This delicate balance between endogenous yolk depletion and successful first feeding is a critical bottleneck in the early life history of this species.

Longevity data for wild-caught individuals, derived from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith annulus counts, indicate that Linguado can survive for up to roughly eleven years [am = up to roughly eleven years] when water temperatures average approximately 16.1 °C [T = 16.1 °C]. This comparatively extended lifespan, relative to other flatfishes of similar body size, is thought to reflect the moderate metabolic demands imposed by the relatively cool, productive waters of the South Brazilian shelf. Females in particular exhibit a gradual senescence pattern, maintaining reproductive capacity well into their later years, with the oldest individuals often producing the largest clutches. The thermal regime of 16.1 °C thus not only shapes growth rates and reproductive output but also modulates the pace of aging, with cooler temperatures potentially extending the functional lifespan by reducing the accumulation of oxidative damage over time.

Comparative studies with other paralichthyid flatfishes reveal that the total length at which female Linguado reach puberty, 39 centimeters [Lp = 39 centimeters], is somewhat larger than values reported for the congeneric species Paralichthys californicus, which matures around 35 centimeters in Californian waters. This difference may reflect local adaptation to the seasonally variable productivity of the southwestern Atlantic, where slower early growth is compensated by a later onset of reproduction and a greater ultimate fecundity. The pubertal mass of 578.4 grams [Wwp = 578.4 grams] marks the point at which females first allocate significant resources to gonadal development, a transition that is histologically identifiable by the appearance of cortical alveoli in the oocytes. Adult females ultimately attain an asymptotic body mass of 6000 grams [Wwi = 6000 grams], which, when compared to the nearly 580 gram pubertal mass, represents a more than tenfold increase in body size — a pattern consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy that prioritizes repeated spawning over multiple seasons.
